title: Explain the three `repartition` variants: `repartition(n)` (round-robin, even distribution), `repartition(*cols)` (hash-modulo on columns, default 200 shuffle partitions), `repartition(n, *cols)` (hash-modulo into n partitions) — and when do you use each?

s1_definition.profdef: `repartition` is a wide transformation on a Spark DataFrame or RDD that performs a full shuffle to redistribute data across a chosen number of partitions. It comes in three forms: `repartition(n)` distributes records round-robin into `n` evenly sized partitions, `repartition(col...)` applies a hash-modulo on the given columns so all rows sharing a key land in the same partition using the default shuffle partition count, and `repartition(n, col...)` combines both by hashing on the columns into exactly `n` partitions. The choice depends on whether you want raw even balance, co-location by key, or both.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a huge pile of transaction slips and wants to hand them to clerks. `repartition(n)` is like dealing the slips one-by-one to `n` clerks like cards, so every clerk gets the same number but Rajesh's slips may be scattered across many clerks. `repartition("accountId")` is like saying "every slip for the same account must go to the same clerk," so all of Rajesh's slips end up together, using the bank's standard number of counters. `repartition(n, "accountId")` says both things: keep each account together AND use exactly `n` counters.
s1_definition.oneliner: `repartition(n)` balances evenly, `repartition(cols)` groups by key, and `repartition(n, cols)` does both into a fixed count — all three pay for a full shuffle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `repartition` is a wide transformation on a Spark DataFrame or RDD that performs a full shuffle to redistribute data across a chosen number of partitions. It comes in three forms: `repartition(n)` distributes records round-robin into `n` evenly sized partitions, `repartition(col...)` applies a hash-modulo on the given columns so all rows sharing a key land in the same partition using the default shuffle partition count, and `repartition(n, col...)` combines both by hashing on the columns into exactly `n` partitions. The choice depends on whether you want raw even balance, co-location by key, or both.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a huge pile of transaction slips and wants to hand them to clerks. `repartition(n)` is like dealing the slips one-by-one to `n` clerks like cards, so every clerk gets the same number but Rajesh's slips may be scattered across many clerks. `repartition("accountId")` is like saying "every slip for the same account must go to the same clerk," so all of Rajesh's slips end up together, using the bank's standard number of counters. `repartition(n, "accountId")` says both things: keep each account together AND use exactly `n` counters.

**One line to remember:** `repartition(n)` balances evenly, `repartition(cols)` groups by key, and `repartition(n, cols)` does both into a fixed count — all three pay for a full shuffle.

sections.s2_technical:
All three variants are wide transformations, which means they trigger a shuffle: data is written to shuffle files on the map side, transferred across the network, and read on the reduce side. This is the expensive part, and it is the same cost for every variant.

The first variant, `repartition(n)`, uses a round-robin partitioner. Spark takes a running counter and assigns each record to the next partition in turn, wrapping around. For example `df.repartition(8)` produces eight partitions of almost exactly equal size regardless of the data's key distribution. Because it ignores the values entirely, rows with the same account can land in different partitions. You use this when you only care about even balance and parallelism, such as spreading a skewed dataset evenly before a CPU-heavy map operation.

The second variant, `repartition("accountId")` or `repartition(col("accountId"))`, uses a hash partitioner. Spark computes `hash(accountId) % numPartitions` and sends all rows with the same hash to the same partition. The number of partitions here defaults to `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`, which is 200 unless you changed it. For example `df.repartition(col("accountId"))` guarantees every transaction for SAV2001 sits in one partition, which is exactly what a later `groupBy("accountId")` wants so it does not shuffle again. The downside is that if one account is a hot key, its partition becomes huge — hash partitioning does not balance, it co-locates.

The third variant, `repartition(16, col("accountId"))`, is the hash partitioner but into a specific number you choose instead of the default 200. For example `df.repartition(16, col("accountId"))` co-locates by account into exactly 16 partitions. You use this when you want key co-location but also want to control the partition count — for instance to match the parallelism of a downstream join or to avoid creating 200 tiny files on write.

A senior-level nuance is that `repartition(cols)` is the one people forget uses 200 partitions by default, which can silently create 200 output files. If you only wanted co-location and a sensible file count, prefer the `repartition(n, cols)` form so the count is explicit.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a nightly job over the day's transactions. After a heavy filter that keeps only high-value transfers, the data is spread across 200 almost-empty partitions with a few holding most rows. The next step is a CPU-heavy fraud score computed per record, and the uneven partitions mean a few tasks run long while most finish instantly. This is exactly what `repartition(n)` fixes — a round-robin reshuffle into, say, 8 even partitions gives every task equal work.

Problem 2 — Later the job must compute per-account totals with a `groupBy("accountId")`. If the data is not already grouped by account, the groupBy triggers its own shuffle. This is exactly what `repartition("accountId")` prevents — pre-partitioning by the account key means all of an account's rows are already co-located, so the groupBy can aggregate without another network shuffle.

Problem 3 — The final write must produce a controlled number of files partitioned by account for a downstream join that uses 16 partitions. This is exactly what `repartition(16, "accountId")` does — it co-locates by account into exactly 16 partitions so the output aligns with the consumer.

The demo simulates these three decisions on a small in-memory list of transactions for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), printing how records map to partitions under each variant so you can see round-robin even balance versus hash co-location.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: six transactions — T1, T2, T4 for SAV2001 (Rajesh) and T3, T5, T6 for CUR3001 (Priya).

Step 1: The demo loads all six transactions into a single in-memory list, standing in for one Spark partition holding the whole dataset.

Step 2: For the even-balance goal, the round-robin partitioner assigns record index 0 to partition 0, index 1 to partition 1, index 2 to partition 2, index 3 back to partition 0, and so on. The data ends perfectly balanced — two records per partition — but Rajesh's three transactions are scattered across all three partitions.

Step 3: For the key-colocation goal, the hash partitioner computes `floorMod(hash(accountId), 4)`. Every SAV2001 row produces the same index, and every CUR3001 row produces the same index, so Rajesh's rows all land together and Priya's rows all land together. The count stays at the default (represented here as 4).

Step 4: For the fixed-count colocation goal, the same hashing runs but modulo 2, so the two accounts map into exactly two partitions while remaining co-located.

Step 5: The log shows each transaction with its destination partition under all three variants, making the difference between balance and co-location visible.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Repartition always performs a full shuffle, and it comes in three forms that differ by how records are placed. The first form, repartition with just a number, uses a round-robin partitioner that deals records evenly like cards into exactly that many partitions. The result is perfectly balanced sizes, but it completely ignores the values, so rows that share a key get scattered. I reach for this when my only concern is even parallelism, for example after a heavy filter that left me with lopsided partitions before a CPU-intensive map.

The second form, repartition with one or more columns, uses a hash partitioner. Spark computes the hash of the key modulo the partition count and sends every row with the same key to the same partition. The important detail that trips people up is that this form uses the default shuffle partition count, which is two hundred, so it can silently produce two hundred partitions and two hundred output files. I use this when I want co-location by key so a downstream groupBy or join on that key does not shuffle again.

The third form, repartition with both a number and columns, is the hash partitioner into an explicit count. It gives me key co-location and control of the partition count at the same time, which is what I want when I need the output to align with a consumer or to avoid too many small files.

In my project at the National Bank of India I used repartition with a plain number to rebalance a skewed daily slice before fraud scoring, repartition on the account column to pre-group transactions so the per-account totals avoided an extra shuffle, and repartition with a count plus the account column to produce exactly sixteen co-located partitions that matched a downstream join. The rule I state in interviews is that a plain number gives balance, columns give co-location at the default count, and the combined form gives both into a count I control, and all three cost a shuffle.
